name: Meadowfoam seed oil

card.summary: A very oxidation-stable plant oil from a Californian/Oregon wildflower, used as a cosmetic emollient with no published human skin-benefit trials.
card.note: Unrefined oil is not considered suitable for eating because of its erucic acid content.

quick.overview:
Meadowfoam seed oil is pressed from the seeds of Limnanthes alba, a small wildflower native to California and Oregon. It is used in cosmetic and hair-care products as an emollient, and is known for being unusually stable against oxidation.

Published work on it is mostly about formulation and chemistry. One 2021 cosmetic-science study tested it as a pigment-dispersing agent in lipstick. No published human trials were found on its effects on skin appearance.
quick.mechanism: Its fatty acids are mostly very long-chain (C20 and C22) types such as eicosenoic and docosadienoic acid, which the sources link to its resistance to going rancid. In products it acts as an emollient and a dispersing agent for pigments.
quick.risks: Reference sources note that unpurified meadowfoam oil is not suitable for human consumption because of high erucic acid. Topical safety data from clinical studies were not found. The plant's commercial crops have been vulnerable to fungal disease.

lead: Meadowfoam seed oil is a vegetable oil obtained from the seeds of Limnanthes alba (white meadowfoam), an annual herb in the family Limnanthaceae native to wet grasslands, vernal pools and moist woodland in California and Oregon.[1] The seeds contain roughly 20 to 30 percent oil, which is made up of more than 98 percent long-chain fatty acids.[1]

In cosmetics and hair care the oil is used for its emollient quality, soft skin feel and stability.[1] Published research on it is largely technical: a 2021 study in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science evaluated it as a natural pigment-dispersing agent in lipstick, compared with castor oil and octyldodecanol.[2] No clinical studies of its effect on human skin or appearance were found.

paras: Reference sources give the main fatty acids of the oil as eicos-5-enoic acid (about 58-64 percent), docosa-5,13-dienoic acid (15-21 percent), erucic acid (10-14 percent) and docos-5-enoic acid (3-6 percent).[1] This long-chain profile is unusual among vegetable oils and is what separates it from most plant oils used in skin care, and it is reported to be most similar to rapeseed oil in composition.[1] Chemists have isolated individual meadowfoam fatty-acid esters, for example by silver-resin chromatography.[3]

The oil is described as among the most oxidatively stable vegetable oils known, which the source attributes mainly to its long-chain fatty acid content.[1] It can also be converted into waxes and lubricants.[1]

Meadowfoam oil appears in cosmetic and hair-care formulations for its emollient properties and skin feel.[1] Patent filings describe its use, alone or combined with hydrogenated jojoba oil, in lip glosses and eye liners and in personal-care compositions.[4][5] A 2021 laboratory study found it could disperse a red lake pigment in lipstick and compared it with castor oil and octyldodecanol.[2] A 2011 paper explored blending its methyl esters with biodiesel, showing industrial uses outside cosmetics.[6]

Meadowfoam is grown on a small commercial scale. It is very susceptible to the fungus Botrytis cinerea, and commercial crops were devastated in the 1982 and 1984 growing seasons.[1] Unpurified oil is not considered suitable for human consumption, mainly because of its high erucic acid content.[1]
No studies found. Existing published research concerns oil chemistry and cosmetic formulation, such as the lipstick pigment-dispersion study,[2] rather than outcomes in human skin.

timeline.event: Commercial meadowfoam crops are devastated by Botrytis cinerea; another loss follows in 1984.[1]
A study evaluates meadowfoam seed oil as a pigment dispersant in lipstick.[2]
